articles.title: Pope delivers veiled rebuke of Milei's austerity measures
articles.summary: Pope Leo made the comments as he arrived in Argentina on the second leg of his Latin America tour.

blocks.text: Pope Leo XIV has said Argentina's economy must benefit everyone including the poor, in a diplomatic but pointed critique of President Javier Milei's austerity measures.
The Pope was speaking as he arrived in Buenos Aires, the second stop on a 12-day tour of Latin America, only three weeks after having had surgery for lung cancer.
In response, right-wing leader Milei said his government was working to avoid "punishing the Argentines of tomorrow in order to benefit the Argentines of today".

This leg of the Pope's journey was expected be the most politically sensitive, with the president's agenda of slashing public spending having been denounced by the Catholic Church for hitting the poorest hardest.
"The economy must be at the service of the people, rather than people being at the service of the economy," Pope Leo said.

He stressed the plight of those who, "despite hard work, nonetheless struggle to meet their household's needs", and urged that "particular concern be shown for those affected by illness, dependency and disability" - a veiled reference to the government's controversial cuts to disability assistance.
In what appeared to be a rebuke of Milei's combative style and language, the Pope said strengthening democracy required a "willingness to listen" and the "careful use of words".
Milei had been particularly outspoken about Leo's predecessor Pope Francis, whom he called "evil on earth" and a "communist" for promoting a doctrine of social justice to help the poor.
On Sunday, however, Milei struck a conciliatory tone, calling Francis an "exceptional figure" and "undoubtedly the most important Argentine in history".
He was also keen to welcome the current Pope earlier, writing in a post on X that Argentina awaits "with immense joy".

Pope Leo urged Argentina to safeguard its democracy. "Those who exercise authority have a duty to act with prudence, to acknowledge the limits of the power entrusted to them, and to direct their decisions toward the good of the entire community," he said.

In his own address welcoming Leo to Argentina, Milei defended his libertarian policies, saying the rights to life, liberty and property are the backbone of Argentina's constitution and of Western democracies.
The Argentine leader, who has said he will seek re-election next year, is a strong supporter of US President Donald Trump, who has criticised Pope Leo for his opposition to the Iran war.
Pope Leo's trip to Argentina has been described as a homage to Francis, who did not return to his homeland during his own papacy.

The Vatican says no extraordinary measures are being taken in relation to the Pope's health, describing him as a "71-year-old who has undergone an operation" not someone with a "permanent medical condition".
Last month's operation to remove a tumour was successful and his doctors say the cancer has not spread.

articles.title: Macalintal to seek SC reconsideration of BSKE ruling
articles.summary: Election lawyer Romulo Macalintal on Monday said he would file a motion for reconsideration (MR) of the Supreme Court's decision upholding the law that postponed the Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan…

blocks.text: Published November 9, 2026 1:02pm

Election lawyer Romulo Macalintal on Monday said he would file a motion for reconsideration (MR) of the Supreme Court's decision upholding the law that postponed the Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE) and extended the term of incumbent barangay officials.
"Ako'y maghahain ng motion for reconsideration at iyan ay pinapayagan sa ating rules," Macalintal told Super Radyo dzBB.
(I will file a motion for reconsideration, which is allowed under our rules.)
Macalintal said he plans to file the motion this week.
"Inaayos ko na lamang yung presentation, yung format ng gagawin ko whether to ask for a total MR or a partial MR na kung saan bibigyan ko ng win-win formula ang ating SC sa bagay na ito," he said.
(I'm just finalizing the presentation and format of my motion, whether to seek a full or partial reconsideration, in which I will offer the SC a win-win formula.)

He said he may ask the SC to uphold its ruling that declared unconstitutional the provision of Republic Act No. 12326 granting Congress the authority to fix the term of office, while maintaining its ruling on the provision postponing the elections.

"Maaari natin sabihin sa SC na 'okay, you declared unconstitutional yung RA 12326 na nagbibigay ng kapangyarihan na to fix the term of office' pero declared naman na unconstitutional yung bahaging nagpo-postpone ng halalan" so parehong panalo. Panalo ang kongreso, panalo ang tao," he added.

(We can tell the SC that it declared unconstitutional the provision of RA 12326 granting the authority to fix the term of office, while also declaring unconstitutional the portion postponing the elections. That way, both sides win. Congress wins, and the people win.)
In a 33-page decision, the SC dismissed Macalintal's petition challenging the constitutionality of the law.

The High Court said the law's primary purpose was to fix the term of office rather than postpone the elections. It also ruled that the guidelines established in its 2023 decision on a petition filed by Macalintal did not apply to the case.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed Republic Act No. 12326 into law in September, effectively postponing the BSKE, setting the term of office of barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan officials at five years and moving the next elections to 2028.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Robredo rules out presidential run anew: 'It's really closed'
articles.summary: The Naga mayor says her decision not to return to national politics came with her 2025 mayoral run and cannot be changed.

blocks.text: November 9, 2026 | 12:56pm
Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo speaks at a local event on Tuesday, Nov. 18, 2025.
Leni Gerona Robredo via Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo again ruled out a run for the presidency in 2028 a year before the filing of candidacies, saying the matter was now "closed" and that she lacked the political savvy needed to navigate national politics.
Robredo said she had settled the matter before running for mayor in 2025, and would not return to national office even if she later decided to leave City Hall.
"It's really closed. Nothing can change that," Robredo said in Bikol in a radio interview on Monday, November 9.
Robredo has resolved not to use the mayoralty as a stepping stone toward 2028. "When I ran for mayor, that decision came with it, that I would no longer leave Naga."
Robredo first ruled out a run for the presidency in April in an interview with the same radio station, RMN dwNX Naga, saying she would most likely seek a second term as mayor instead.
Opposition figures, including Sen. Kiko Pangilinan, her 2022 running mate, have since urged her to reconsider.
Early polling for 2028 presidential bets has placed Robredo as a potential frontrunner second to Vice President Sara Duterte, who remains ahead in the surveys.
In a Pulse Asia survey conducted September 17 to 24, which tested a wide field of possible candidates, Duterte was the preference of 50% of those surveyed, while Robredo was at 26%.

Asked about Transportation Secretary Vince Dizon, whose repeated trips to Naga have fed speculation about a 2028 tandem, Robredo said: "[Secretary] Vince has never brought up 2028." She said his visits were tied to the work they had done together in the city.

Dizon has been in Naga several times this year, the most recent being an unannounced visit on October 26, the same day Malacañang moved him from the Department of Public Works and Highways back to the Department of Transportation in a swap with Secretary Giovanni "Banoy" Lopez. Neither side disclosed what was discussed. Dizon has denied that his visits carry a political agenda.

Robredo also said she had not spoken with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. about 2028. She said her last conversation with him was at his birthday celebration in Malacañang in September, which she attended on invitation along with other local chief executives.
The former vice president was also candid in explaining how her years in both national and local office had shown her where she falls short.
"Maybe I could handle the job, but my political savvy really seems lacking," she said. "At the national level, you need to be a strong communicator. I'm weak at that."
She said the next president should be able "not only to do the job but also to handle national politics."
"At the national level, people largely believe what they read, how you're portrayed," she said. In Naga, she said she believes she could better focus on the work without having to play politics.
Robredo served as vice president from 2016 to 2022 after defeating Marcos for the post. She lost the 2022 presidential election to him, receiving 14.8 million votes to his 31 million.
In May 2025, she was elected Naga's first female mayor.

articles.title: Victorian election 2026: Concern and scepticism among Labor MPs as new poll shows party trailing One Nation
articles.summary:
Ben Carroll refuses to be drawn on latest opinion poll that puts Labor at all-time low of just 18%, behind One Nation on 21% and the Coalition on 33%

  • Get our

blocks.text: Victorian Labor MPs are both sceptical and seriously concerned about a new poll ahead of the state election showing the party trailing third behind One Nation, with its primary vote at an all-time low of just 18%.

The DemosAU/PremierNational, first published by the Herald Sun on Monday, showed Labor’s primary vote share has crashed seven points to 18%, putting it in third place behind the Coalition’s 33% and One Nation’s 21%. At the same time, the Greens improved their primary vote to 17%, an increase of three points since September.
It means the Coalition now leads Labor on a two-party preferred basis 56-44, compared with 52-48 in September.

DemosAU’s head of research, George Hasanakos, said if the poll were replicated on election night, many contests across the state would be between the Liberals or Nationals and One Nation, which would then result in a “clear Coalition majority”.
“If that happens, One Nation has to poll really, really well to have a chance of winning, because Labor and Greens preferences will flow to the Liberals,” he said.

On election night, the Victorian electoral commission plans to conduct a two-candidate-preferred count, or 2CP, between the two candidates it expects to finish with the most support after preferences are distributed. They are selecting the indicative 2CP for each seat based on on polling, analysis of preference flows and results from previous, which will not publish this before election day to avoid influencing voter behaviour.
Hasanakos added that he “double, triple, quadruple checked” the result of the “extraordinary” poll, which had 1,562 respondents, an effective sample of 818 and a margin of error of 3.4%.
“We went to the trouble of a bigger sample here, and I stand by it,” he said.
Ben Carroll repeatedly refused to say whether he was worried about the poll at a press conference in South Melbourne on Monday morning.

“What I’m focused on every day is fighting for working people and making sure that every Victorian that goes into the ballot on November 28 knows that under my government you have a government on your side that will fight for you,” he told reporters.
“The alternative is a Liberal-One Nation government that will fight against you – they’re going to shrink the economy, cause a recession and make life difficult for every single Victorian.”

But the result has sparked serious concerns among the Labor caucus, even though some MPs are sceptical about the 18% figure. Inside Labor’s campaign headquarters, they are treating the result as an “outlier” and point to other public polls that have their primary vote in the 20s.
Several Labor MPs, unauthorised to speak publicly, have told Guardian Australia there are many in the caucus questioning their party’s strategy.

This includes a focus in recent days on crime – an issue that is typically a Coalition strength. On Sunday, Carroll announced a $204m plan to enable judges to sentence low- and mid-level youth offenders to a new rehabilitation detention program while on Monday he announced $70m to recruit 200 more police reservists to re-open stations and build and upgrade more stations.

“Caucus is really angry and deflated, because this is all happening because of him,” one MP
“Even if it’s higher than 18, and we get back into something with a 2 in front of it, the experiment has been an epic fail, the campaign is in freefall, and it’s about to get a whole lot worse.”
Another MP said the focus on crime was “diabolically stupid strategy” as the government had years to tackle community concern around rising rates.

The opposition leader, Jess Wilson, on Monday said her party had a focus on “getting tough on crime”, including by introducing Aidan’s Law, to toughen sentencing for attacks on people who step in to protect others.

Carroll immediately matched the commitment to introduce the proposed law, named after 22-year-old Aidan Becker, who was fatally stabbed at Mernda station after stepping in to protect a 14-year-old during an alleged violent robbery.
It comes as Pauline Hanson rejected reports by The Age and 60 Minutes on Sunday that her former national campaign director, Sean Black, continues to secretly work for One Nation in Victoria.

Black was in 2018 was jailed for rape and subsequently lost his appeal against the conviction but was then rehired by One Nation in 2020 as a campaign director after serving his time. Hanson sacked him after political pressure earlier this year.
She told the Australian Financial Review on Monday “the day that I sacked him [Sean Black] that was the day he finished up”.

articles.title: PNP: Focus crimes down by 32% in July-October 2026
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police (PNP) has recorded a 32% decrease in focus crimes nationwide from July to October 2026, PNP chief Police General Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said Monday.

blocks.text: Published November 9, 2026 12:37pm
The Philippine National Police (PNP) has recorded a 32% decrease in focus crimes nationwide from July to October 2026, PNP chief Police General Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said Monday.
Focus crimes are offenses considered serious in nature and occur with sufficient frequency and regularity.
These include murder, homicide, physical injury, rape, robbery, theft, carnapping of motor vehicles, and carnapping of motorcycles.
At a press briefing, Nartatez said the PNP recorded 9,047 focus crime incidents, which was down by 4,354 cases or 32% from the 13,401 incidents reported in the same period last year.
“Our latest figures show a downward trend in focus crimes over the past four months,” he said.
“From July to October 2026, the PNP recorded 9,047 focus crimes incidents nationwide, down by 4,354 cases, or 32%, from the 13,401 cases recorded in the same period last year,” he added.
Nartatez said the decline reflected the daily efforts of police personnel to keep communities safe.
Meanwhile, the PNP conducted 5,101 anti-illegal drug operations in October, resulting in the arrest of 5,788 individuals and the confiscation of illegal drugs worth around P192.7 million.
The police also arrested 8,839 wanted persons nationwide during the same period, including 2,353 most wanted persons and 6,486 other wanted persons.
In its campaign against loose firearms, the PNP arrested 1,018 individuals, accounted for 4,126 firearms, and took custody of another 3,339 firearms for safekeeping.
The PNP also conducted 4,506 anti-illegal gambling operations, leading to the arrest of 10,289 individuals.

In its anti-smuggling campaign, police conducted 2,927 operations, resulting in 635 arrests and the confiscation of suspected smuggled goods and equipment worth around P646.67 million. — RSJ, GMA News

Senate PRIB

MANILA, Philippines — The Senate impeachment court has kept the three withdrawn impeachment articles against Vice President Sara Duterte under its gag rule, reversing an earlier ruling that had opened them to public discussion.
Presiding Officer Chiz Escudero reiterated the ruling as Duterte's impeachment trial resumed Monday, November 9.

Under the ruling, the sub judice principle in Rule XVIII of the Rules of Procedure on Impeachment Trials applies "with equal force to all articles of impeachment, whether withdrawn or pending adjudication."

The court also reiterated its August 26 order directing covered persons, including prosecutors, defense lawyers and senator-judges, to refrain from publicly discussing the merits of the impeachment case.
The ruling reverses Escudero's earlier position that the restriction would no longer apply to the three articles withdrawn by House prosecutors in October.
Defense lead counsel Sheila Sison had objected to lifting the restriction, while Senator-Judge Francis Pangilinan filed a motion for reconsideration.
The court also considered a November 4 manifestation from Duterte stating that she was not waiving the protection of Rule XVIII.

Next witnesses. The impeachment court also ordered the issuance of subpoenas to three prospective defense witnesses: lawyer Anel Martin Antero, Chadrin Parian and Quezon City prosecutor Vimar Barcellano.
The court also granted the defense's request to move the appearance of lawyer Suzette Balucanag-Punay from Monday to Tuesday, November 10.
In a November 6 manifestation, the defense informed the court that Balucanag-Punay could not testify on opening day because of a scheduled magnetic resonance imaging examination.

articles.title: CFMEU ‘enjoy a significant level of influence’ over Victorian government, Big Build royal commission hears
articles.summary:
Inquiry into allegations of corruption begins block of hearings focused on 2022 level crossing removal project

  • Get our

blocks.text: The royal commission into allegations of corruption on Victorian Big Build projects has heard a major construction company feared putting the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union (CFMEU) offside because of its close links to the Daniel Andrews Labor government.

The first block of hearings under the commission into the integrity of major public and civil infrastructure construction projects in Victoria will hear evidence about the union’s involvement in a level crossing removal project at Gap Road in Sunbury, north of Melbourne, in 2022.
The project involved the removal of a level crossing and the construction of a new rail bridge and underpass.
The counsel assisting the commission, Chris Young KC, said 20 witnesses have been compelled to appear during the November hearings.

But he warned that others were not complying with orders to produce documents to the commission, including using the excuse of “government policy” to delay their production. Failing to comply with such orders is a criminal offence.
“It is extremely concerning that some parties have not complied with the terms of those notices to produce,” Young said.
The hearings in November will focus on what government officials did during a June 2022 meeting in order to appease the union, who had forced work to stop on the Gap Road project.

Young showed the commission evidence that – in the years before the union interfered in the project – there was increasing awareness within the construction sector about the prospect of industrial action curtailing work, and the growing influence of the CFMEU.
He said that in 2017, one of the companies involved in the Gap Road project, John Holland, noted that the CFMEU was “proud of the fact that none of their site visits are code compliant”.

It also noted in an email the “significance of the CFMEU relationship with the Andrews government in Victoria, and the impact this is having, and will have in the future, in respect of client relationships with the Victorian government”.

Such was the extent of that relationship that John Holland officials suspected the CFMEU would have a “substantial amount of knowledge around proposed government tenders and input” in respect of the tender process.
“We are thus particularly mindful of the optics in our interactions with union stakeholders,” the 2017 email said.

Four years later, the construction company noted that “the CFMEU are emboldened by their success on major infrastructure projects,” and later in 2021, that they “enjoy a significant level of influence within the state government”.
“It is a level of influence not seen in previous years and is unlikely to diminish.”
Police called to dispute
Young told the hearing that four of the CFMEU officials who would later force work to stop at Gap Road had similarly interfered in the Metro Tunnel project.

He said the officials entered the Gap Road project’s eastern portal 29 times in January 2020, and were involved in activity considered to be unlawful, but nonetheless received attention from the government, which asked if the safety issues they raised were valid.
Young said that a “very high risk rating” was applied to the possibility of industrial action on Gap Road.
But he said that it was not until May 2022 where this risk escalated, and CFMEU officials more regularly appeared on site.

By early June, the health and safety manager for the Rail Network Alliance involved in the project, Neil Thompson, was calling police, desperate for their help in removing union officials who were stopping work including by sitting on barriers and refusing to move.

Young tendered internal notes taken on the union activity that showed there were references to the CFMEU officials warning workers that “you guys better not turn up tonight otherwise we will smash you during the day,” and that “their life would be [made] very difficult for them personally” if they continued working on the project.

A recording of a phone call between Thompson and WorkSafe and a subsequent email showed that on 6 June – the day before a meeting that is central to the commission’s hearings – he was unclear about how to get work to continue on site.
Thompson stressed the need for the union to be removed, given trains had been stopped on the line in order for a bridge to be built.
“We actually called Victoria police to escort themself off site,” Thompson said in the call to WorkSafe.
“Victoria police said there was nothing they could do. We’re going around in circles a bit because last week WorkSafe said there was nothing they could do.
after newsletter promotion
“We’re just having to put up with no work happening at the moment.”
The following day, Young said, there was a 13-minute meeting, followed by a subsequent meeting at the CFMEU, which resolved the issues.
Two CFMEU officials, Joe Myles and Paul Tzimas, attended the meeting along with four officials from the project, Young told the hearing.

Young said that while the commission had obtained significant documentation regarding the events leading up to the meeting, little was known about what occurred during it and why it was significant, so the commission would be reliant on the memory witnesses had of conversations four years ago.
The key questions included what stopped the work, and whether those disruptions were used as leverage by the CFMEU, he said.
It remained unclear exactly how much the CFMEU disruption to works on the site had cost, nor what the cost was to end the disruption, Young said.

But the union interrupted work on the site for 36 hours – and traffic controllers employed after the disruption charged significantly more than those previously employed, documents in evidence before the commission show.
The hourly rate increased from about $45 to $88, or from $59 to $147 for penalty rates, the documents show.
This meant, for example, that one 10-and-a-half hour shift cost $609 under the previous firm, but $1225 for the same shift under the new firm, Young said.

The Major Transport Infrastructure Authority director general started considering the cost implications of a CFMEU campaign to increase the rates of traffic controllers about the same time the disruptions occurred on the Gap Road project.

A September briefing prepared for the then minister for transport infrastructure, Jacinta Allan, estimated that the changes could cost the authority $60m to $78m for current projects, and well in excess of $400m for those projects in planning.

blocks.caption: Premier Ben Carroll says ‘I want every Victorian to get the answers they deserve’. Photograph: Jay Kogler/AAP

blocks.text: Royal commission that ‘Victorians deserve’
Earlier on Monday, the premier, Ben Carroll, said the royal commission was one “that Victoria needed and Victorians deserve”.
“I want every Victorian to get the answers they deserve,” Carroll said.

“This is a royal commission for Victoria. It’s a tough royal commission. It’s truly independent – [it has] the broadest terms of reference possible, a special prosecutor established as well. I said I’d do this in my first press conference and now it is up and running as it should be.”
Carroll confirmed legal representation for two former premiers, Jacinta Allan and Daniel Andrews, was “supported by the state” as has been the case at “other previous royal commissions”.

The opposition leader, Jess Wilson, said: “They’ve trashed the future of this state, and now Ben Carroll is allowing the taxpayer to foot the bill for them to be defended in the royal commission, it doesn’t pass the pub test.”
The hearing continues.
– Additional reporting by Benita Kolovos

The Philippine National Police (PNP) has received more than 500 pieces of information regarding the whereabouts of former senator Ronald "Bato" dela Rosa, PNP chief Police General Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said Monday.
At a press briefing, Nartatez said the information had been validated and acted upon, prompting police operations in various parts of the country.
“There are not less than 500 information na dumating na and those were properly validated, pinuntahan po natin at in-operate po natin,” he said.
(There are not less than 500 information that have arrived and those were properly validated, we went there and operated.)
“From Western, Eastern Mindanao, Visayas, Bicol, Southern Tagalog, Northern or Central Luzon. And even island that I haven't heard na ngayon ko lang narinig at inikot ng ating mga police,” he added.
(From Western, Eastern Mindanao, Visayas, Bicol, Southern Tagalog, Northern or Central Luzon. And even islands that I haven't heard of, I just heard about it and our police went there.)
However, Dela Rosa was not found in the locations operated by the police as authorities continue the manhunt against the senator.
The PNP had deployed tracker teams and other personnel to pursue leads concerning Dela Rosa's whereabouts.
Nartatez said the police are working with other law enforcement agencies and intelligence units to implement arrest warrants against wanted individuals.
Dela Rosa is wanted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) in connection with the crimes against humanity case arising from former President Rodrigo Duterte’s war on drugs.
The senator is accused of being a co-perpetrator in the alleged crimes.

Earlier, the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) claimed that Dela Rosa was hiding in Mindanao under the protection of an “armed and powerful group,” but did not identify the group.
A P50-million reward is being offered for information that would lead to the senator’s arrest. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: G7 ministers meet as Europe seeks greater say in Ukraine peace talks
articles.summary: With Washington preparing negotiations with Moscow and Kyiv, European leaders fear Ukraine could face pressure to accept a bad deal. Iran tensions and the threat of renewed US strikes are also on the…

image.caption: The G7 meeting coincides with US-mediated talks between Moscow and Kyiv in Abu Dhabi scheduled to begin on Tuesday [FILE: March 13, 2024]Image: Andriy Andriyenko/SOPA Images/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Foreign ministers from the Group of Seven (G7) leading industrialized nations are set to meet in Paris on Monday and Tuesday for talks on how Europe can be part of US efforts to end Russia’s war on Ukraine and how to urge Washington to not resume military action against Iran.
The meeting will bring together leading diplomats from Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States.
It coincides with US-mediated talks between Moscow and Kyiv in Abu Dhabi scheduled to begin on Tuesday.

European governments are concerned the the US might be pushing Ukraine to a settlement favoring Russia. US President Donald Trump, in the run-up to the Abu Dhabi talks, said a "very big" deal was in the making, suggesting Ukraine could emerge from a settlement with altered ‌borders.

"I think we're gonna have it done, and I think it's ‌gonna happen ​and they're gonna end up with a little bit different shape Ukraine," Trump told broadcaster CBS. The US president also said the deal would involve all of Europe.

blocks.caption: European leaders fear that Putin may have too much influence over the Trump administrationImage: Dmitry Azarov/Kommersant Photo/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Europe insists it's at the table
About the talks in Abu Dhabi, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot told RTL radio that "Europeans will be represented and France will participate in these talks."

European leaders have long insisted that any deal to end the war should include the continent's participation in the talks and that any settlement should not come at the expense of Ukraine's sovereignty.

When asked about the US plans for a possible agreement to end the war in Ukraine, Barrot said he did not know the details but stressed that no deal affecting the European security architecture could be done without the Europeans.
Particular attention at the upcoming meeting will be on US Secretary of State Marco Rubio who will attend both days unlike the last G7 meeting where he came only for one.

Rubio suggested that recent discussions had made progress on security guarantees for Ukraine and the wider European region. Trump's envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner has also described US efforts to develop a broader European security framework.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has in the past expressed doubts over proposals for a new European security framework, suggesting that any such debates should follow, rather than precede, efforts to end the war.
What Trump’s Russia talks could cost Europe
US strategy on Iran remains unclear
The G7 ministers are also expected to discuss US tensions with Iran, as Trump has not ruled out additional military strikes against the country.

Washington has previously considered targeting suspected nuclear facilities, including the site known as Pickaxe Mountain, following the US midterm elections last week. Tehran denies that the location is a nuclear facility.

European governments are seeking a diplomatic resolution rather than a resumption of military action. Gobal attention is particularly on the restoration of normal shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for international energy supplies.
Trump recently said that Iranian officials were keen to reach an agreement, suggesting negotiations remained possible.
The Paris gathering is among the final major diplomatic events of France's G7 presidency. The United States is scheduled to assume the group's rotating presidency in 2027.

articles.title: Trump tells 60 Minutes that deportation policy was ‘too tough’
articles.summary: President makes unusual acknowledgement that one of the defining policies of his second administration had become a political liability

blocks.text: Donald Trump has admitted that his deportation policy was “too tough” and has offered to strike an immigration deal with Democrats in a concession following the Republicans’ disastrous defeat in the midterm elections.

In an interview on the CBS network’s 60 Minutes broadcast on Sunday, the president acknowledged that the aggressive crackdown had hurt him politically and said he was open to an arrangement to allow some undocumented immigrants to remain in the US.

Trump was asked by 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat whether his deportation policy had gone too far. “I think it was too tough,” he said. “I think it might be too tough, yeah. And a lot of people would say that it’s great. But a lot of people think it’s too tough.”

The president’s comments offered an unusually frank acknowledgment that one of the defining policies of his second administration had become a political liability. But they were seemingly at odds with his decision on Friday to elevate Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration crackdown, to White House chief of staff.

Since Trump returned to office, sweeping Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids at workplaces, homes and public spaces have ensnared people with no criminal records, separated families and spread fear in immigrant communities. Federal agents fatally shot two US citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, during operations in Minneapolis earlier this year.

The president claimed that his policy “both helped and hurt”, since people gave him an “A+ for closing up the border” and “very high marks for getting the bad ones out”. But he admitted: “I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally.”

Trump added that there were competing views within the country about whether undocumented immigrants should be deported or allowed to remain if they were working and paying taxes. He said some people believed that “they should be allowed to stay if they’re good people working in a landscaping company” and “in some cases, paying taxes”.

Trump said he believed an agreement with Democrats was achievable, allowing some long-term undocumented residents to stay while continuing to remove people convicted of serious crimes. He proposed targeting killers, rapists and drug dealers while making an accommodation for people who had been in the country for 10 or 15 years.

“Let the people that are here, and in some cases here for 10 and 15 years, work a deal for them,” he said. He described the proposal as something that could be negotiated, saying: “I think that’s something that’s actually doable.”

Trump suggested Democrats were receptive to a compromise, saying some had already contacted him. Asked whether he could refrain from name-calling for six months to secure an agreement, he replied: “Very easily.”

Trump also blamed the war with Iran and higher petrol prices for much of the Republicans’ midterms defeat, agreeing with an assessment by his vice-president, JD Vance, that the conflict had been a major factor. He also cited what he described as growing dislike of Israel.

He maintained, however, that the military campaign had been justified and said he would make the same decision again. “My answer is an emphatic yes because you can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon,” he said.

Trump insisted the war had been won and predicted that Tehran would eventually negotiate a deal. He acknowledged that the military campaign might not have been popular in the short term, saying: “I think historically, this will be a very good decision. Is it a good decision for today and tomorrow? Maybe not.”
He said he was not looking to escalate the conflict after the midterms.

On the economy, the president conceded that his administration had failed to communicate its achievements effectively, despite repeatedly claiming that employment, investment and stock market figures were at record levels. “I think it was bad messaging, maybe by me,” he said.

Trump signalled an openness to safeguards for artificial intelligence, despite having previously favoured allowing technology companies to police themselves rather than imposing sweeping government restrictions. “I don’t mind guardrails,” he told 60 Minutes. “But I don’t wanna put us in a deep second position.”
The interview also raised questions about the substantial increase in Trump’s personal wealth since his return to the White House.

Douthat cited a Forbes estimate that Trump’s net worth had increased by $3bn from the autumn of 2024 to the autumn of 2025. Trump initially suggested that the increase reflected the general performance of the stock market and said his finances were managed by his son.

Asked about his family’s cryptocurrency business, World Liberty Financial, in which he is a co-owner and which has attracted investment from people connected to the United Arab Emirates, Trump defended the arrangement by saying: “I know nothing about it.”

But Dan Alexander, a Forbes senior editor who calculates the net worth of wealthy individuals for the magazine, challenged Trump’s explanation in a lengthy thread on X, arguing that the president’s increased fortune could not be explained simply by stock market gains.

Alexander identified several sources including cryptocurrency ventures that generated more than $1bn in proceeds and the appreciation of tokens retained by Trump, overseas licensing agreements that expanded the value of his branding business, and the removal of an almost $500m financial penalty in his New York civil fraud case.

Trump also offered a glimpse of the Republican succession battle ahead of the 2028 presidential election, saying he might endorse a candidate but had not decided whether to intervene. Asked whether he expected to endorse a successor, Trump replied: “Probably. Not necessarily.”
He described the Republican party as having a strong field of potential candidates and praised secretary of state Marco Rubio while declining to rule out other contenders.

The president said his endorsement would carry considerable weight but suggested he might be better off staying out of the contest. He also expressed confidence that the “Make America great again” movement could survive without him as its leader, describing its defining principles as strong borders and a strong military.

At the end of the interview, Trump was asked whether he could forgive political opponents including former FBI director James Comey and former House speaker Nancy Pelosi, even before the judgment of God. Trump said: “The answer is no. I want to be honest, no.”

Douthat followed up: “Mr President. You have had the most charmed and remarkable life of any American in my entire lifetime and you are telling me that before the judgment throne of God you couldn’t find it in your heart to forgive some of your enemies? After all that’s been given to you? Come on. Help me out here.”
But Trump remained adamant, insisting: “I probably cannot do that, no, because I do hate some of my enemies and I always will.”
Douthat then noted that many presidents are remembered with a single line such as “He freed the slaves” or “He won the cold war” and asked what line will Trump’s presidency be remembered with.
The president said simply: “That I made America great again.”

articles.title: Who is Engr. Jaime Adalin, the first witness of the defense?
articles.summary: The defense panel on Monday began the presentation of evidence in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, with Davao City assessor Engr. Jaime Adalin first to be called to the witness…

blocks.text: Published November 9, 2026 11:40am

The defense panel on Monday began the presentation of evidence in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, with Davao City assessor Engr. Jaime Adalin first to be called to the witness stand.
Defense counsel Lindon Bacquel presented the offer of testimony for Adalin, pointing out that as a city assessor, the witness has personal knowledge of tax declarations.
Adalin said that he is a civil engineer and a real estate appraiser. He is also a resident of Cabantian, Davao City, for around 10 years now.
He said he has been working as the Davao City assessor for more or less nine years, where he is tasked with ensuring that “all laws governing real properties shall be properly executed.”
He said he is also responsible for establishing a systematic real property assessment, as well as issuing certifications pertaining to records of assessment and other relevant information.

In the offer, Bacquel said Adalin is expected to prove that the House prosecution panel’s claim that the Vice President failed to disclose the real property covered by Transfer Certificate of Title (TCT) 146-2024010775 in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN) was “malicious and completely false.”

Private prosecutor Benjamin Tolosa Jr., on the other hand, argued that “there is no way” that Adalin could prove that the property indicated in Duterte’s SALN was the same property covered by the subject TCT.
The prosecution likewise opposed the characterization that their position that the property covered by the TCT was not disclosed in Duterte’s SALN was maliciously and completely false.

“We take the strongest exception to this accusation, Your Honor. It cannot be said that it is completely false because just a mere facial examination of those two documents would show that there are obvious discrepancies between the two,” Tolosa said. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: ‘Outrageous and racist’: premier responds to NSW One Nation candidate’s claim Australians are being ‘demographically replaced’
articles.summary:
Chris Minns and human rights commissioner lambast comments made by Stuart Bonds, who leads party’s NSW upper house ticket

  • Get our

blocks.text: The New South Wales premier and the Australian Human Rights Commission have criticised comments by the man who heads One Nation’s upper house ticket in NSW after he said Australians faced demographic replacement unless “mass migration” was curtailed.
Chris Minns described Stuart Bonds’ comments as “frankly outrageous and racist”.
Minns said the replacement theory being espoused by Bonds was “just a conspiracy theory that’s been imported from the US here to Australia”.
Bonds will be the first candidate on the rightwing party’s NSW upper house ticket and on current polling is likely to be elected in March’s state election.
He made the incendiary remarks at an anti-immigration rally in Sydney’s CBD on Sunday. Several hundred people attended amid a sea of Australian flags.

At least one neo-Nazi, Joel Davis, was spotted among them, as well as rightwing figures including the national director of the Family First party, Lyle Shelton, who was previously head of the Australian Christian Lobby.
“Make no mistake, we are being demographically replaced inside our own nation,” Bonds told attendees after referring to abortion rates in Europe, the US and Australia.
“If we don’t support Australian mothers having Australian children, we are going to pay for other cultures’ children to be brought up in our lands.”
He warned that unless it was stopped it would be “impossible to reverse”.
Bonds told the crowd that a country was “a shared culture, a shared border, a shared flag, a shared language and a dominant religion”.
“After 240 years, we are told we’re still on stolen land, and we’re meant to apologise for being here,” he said.

“Yet, in the same vein, we’re expected to believe that an immigrant arriving yesterday is as Australian as you and me. I don’t accept that people like the Bondi shooters are as Australian as you and me. I don’t accept that.”
The race discrimination commissioner, Giridharan Sivaraman, said comments that some Australians were superior to others sowed “division and hate”.
“The idea that migrants can never truly be Australian ignores both our history and our shared future,” he said on Monday.

“Australia has always been shaped by successive generations of people who came here from around the world and helped build the nation we know today. It has the longest continuous culture in the world.
“Throughout history, periods of uncertainty have often seen minority communities cast as scapegoats. Today, migrants are too frequently portrayed as the cause of Australia’s challenges.

“Reducing complex problems to a simple narrative that migrants are to blame is not only inaccurate, it risks fuelling division, exclusion and racism. Migrants are not separate from the Australian story. They are central to it.”
after newsletter promotion
Bonds told the rally that the “socialist plan” was to “destroy and bring down and tear down the fabric of your civilisation” pointing to European countries “on fire”.
He said Australia was going down a path “of becoming a special economic zone within Asia,” and that it needed to “re-establish ourselves as a proud Australian nation”.
Minns said voters should ask themselves which portfolio Bonds would have were One Nation to win the election.
“Trade, education, Treasury? I mean, what job will this bloke have in a Coalition-One Nation government?” Minns said.
“And are we going to see some distancing from those kind of views and those horrific perspectives or points of view from the Coalition?”
Comment was sought from the Coalition’s spokesperson on multiculturalism, Mark Coure, and from One Nation’s NSW headquarters.
Bonds’ comments were also reverberating in Canberra.
The federal minister for multicultural affairs, Anne Aly, said Australians with migrant backgrounds were not replacing Australians – they simply were Australians.
“Questioning someone’s right to belong because of their race or ancestry is not a debate about immigration,” she said.
“It’s divisive, dangerous and goes against everything we stand for as Australians.”
– Additional reporting by Australian Associated Press

articles.summary: Two US fishermen say they spotted the man treading water around 20 miles (32km) off the Californian coast.

blocks.text: A cruise ship pianist was found treading water around 20 miles (32km) off the Californian coast after falling overboard, according to US media reports.

Two fishermen discovered the Royal Caribbean employee near Catalina Island on Friday and officials believe he may have been in the Pacific Ocean for nine hours, according to CBS News, the BBC's US news partner.
"I'm like, 'Yeah, it's a human being. Stop the boat; let's get all of our lines in," Grant Garrett was quoted as saying, recalling the moment he and Sean Norton spotted him.
The man, who has not yet been identified, was taken to hospital in a stable condition, the US Coast Guard told the BBC, adding it was investigating the incident.
The fishermen say the man identified himself as a pianist on a 14-deck cruise ship called the Ovation of the Seas.
"The only thing he said to me was, 'Thank you. I thought I was gonna die,'" Norton said.
The Coast Guard said in a statement it had received a report from "a Good Samaritan who recovered a conscious individual from the water".
The person was handed over to Newport Beach Lifeguards, who confirmed he was an employee of the Ovation of the Seas cruise ship, it said.
Lifeguard officials believe he may have fallen overboard at around 02:30, about nine hours before he was discovered.
"It was approximately 15 to 20 miles offshore, pretty much in the middle of the ocean," Newport Beach Lifeguard Battalion Chief Adam Yacenda told CBS.
Norton credited the man's survival to unusually warm ocean temperatures.
"You have this crazy super El Niño year. This guy was in the water for probably 10 hours, but the water's 76 degrees," Norton said, which equates to about 24C.
"A different year, no way he makes it," Norton said.
The developing El Niño climate phenomenon is now the strongest on record, according to scientists monitoring the Pacific, with ocean temperatures about 3.05C above average.
In a statement to the BBC, a Royal Caribbean Group spokesperson said: "We are providing support and assistance to our crew member during this difficult time.
"To respect the privacy of our employee, we have no additional details to share."

articles.title: Pope Leo delivers stinging rebuke of Milei’s austerity measures during Argentina visit
articles.summary:
Pontiff tells Argentina’s president the economy must benefit all on second stop of 12-day Latin America tour

Pope Leo XIV has delivered a stinging critique of Argentine president Javier…

blocks.text: Pope Leo XIV has delivered a stinging critique of Argentine president Javier Milei’s harsh austerity measures, insisting growth must benefit all in a speech met with rapturous applause in Buenos Aires.

“The economy must be at the service of the people, rather than people being at the service of the economy,” he said on Sunday, shortly after landing in Argentina on the second leg of a Latin America tour.
Leo stressed the plight of those who, “despite hard work, nonetheless struggle to meet their household’s needs”.

He spoke out in defence of the poor and pensioners, insisting that “particular concern be shown for those affected by illness, dependency and disability” – a veiled reference to the government’s controversial cuts to disability assistance.
He also told Milei, known for his foul-mouthed diatribes, that strengthening democracy required a “willingness to listen” and the “careful use of words”.
Leo, 71, is on an ambitious 12-day tour of the continent, just three weeks after undergoing surgery for lung cancer.
The visit is the first by a pontiff to Argentina in nearly four decades, and Leo was met with calls to help mend deep divisions in the country after three years of austerity under Milei.
Argentina is the home country of the late pope, Francis, who Milei famously insulted for his pro-poor teachings.
Leo said he was “retracing” Francis’s steps.
Argentines are hoping the leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics will help unite the country, which is bitterly divided between supporters and opponents of Milei.

“Just like the World Cup unites us, hopefully the pope will too,” said Liliana Deblauwe, a 68-year-old retired teacher who waited with hundreds of people to see the pope visit a monument to liberation hero Jose de San Martin.
Hundreds more chanting “Papa Leon” (Spanish for Leo) gathered outside the presidential palace, where he was hosted by Milei.
Brian Inacio Rodriguez, a 26-year-old job seeker, spent five days travelling overland from Ushuaia, at the very tip of South America, to see the pontiff.
He said he hoped he brought “much peace to Argentina”.

blocks.caption: Pope Leo alongside Argentine foreign minister, Pablo Quirno, after laying a wreath in Plaza San Martin in Buenos Aires. Photograph: Matias Martin Campaya/EPA

blocks.text: Leo arrived in Buenos Aires from Uruguay, where he began his first trip as pope to Latin America, the world’s most Catholic continent which is becoming increasingly secular.
In Uruguay, he condemned drug violence and urged an end to child poverty.
In Buenos Aires, he insisted on the importance of “personal integrity” in public office, stressing that “corruption undermines the confidence of citizens in their institutions.”
The Argentine stage of his visit aims to boost the flagging faith of a country left disappointed by Francis’s failure to visit during his papacy.
It will also act as a litmus test of support for the church. In a recent University of Buenos Aires poll, 57.7% of people identified as Catholic, down from about 90% in the 1960s.
Leo will visit a home for disabled people and a prison and celebrate three open-air masses.
The church has said it expects 7 million to attend the various events.

Milei came to office on a promise to revive Argentina’s ailing economy and tame runaway inflation by shrinking the welfare state, targeting public hospitals, universities and pensioners in particular.
The poverty rate has swung wildly since he came to power – increasing to 32.3% in September.
A close ally of US president Donald Trump, with a similar combative style, Milei had a tense relationship with Francis.
On the campaign trail the cost-cutting economist called his countryman an “imbecile” for championing social justice.
Once in office, however, he softened his tone, but he continues to heap insults on the press and opposition.
His relationship with Leo has so far been cordial, but the local Catholic church has heavily criticised him for treating key social services solely as a budgetary constraint.
Milei has also been criticised for restricting several democratic freedoms, including the right to protest. But he maintains a loyal supporter base for drastically reducing inflation.

articles.title: Major fuel price rollbacks set Nov. 10 with gasoline seen to fall P16.8
articles.summary: Motorists face sharply lower pump prices Tuesday.

blocks.text: November 9, 2026 | 10:00am
Passenger buses are seen on a road with other motorists in Manila on Sept. 22, 2026.
AFP / Ted Aljibe
MANILA, Philippines — Motorists can finally expected sharply lower pump prices Tuesday, led by a P16.80-per-liter cut in gasoline after several weeks of mixed adjustments.
The Department of Energy announced the following changes Monday, November 9:

items: Gasoline: down P16.80 per liter
Diesel: down P4.10 per liter
Kerosene: down P3.70 per liter

blocks.text: The new prices are expected to remain in effect through Monday, November 16.
The rollback follows last week's P3.50-per-liter increase in gasoline. Diesel and kerosene prices fell by P1 and P1.90 per liter, respectively.
Industry forecasts late last week had pointed to smaller cuts, particularly for gasoline. The DOE has yet to clarify whether the reductions will be implemented in full Tuesday or staggered.
Global oil prices have come under pressure as concerns eased over further U.S. strikes on Iran following Democratic gains in the midterm elections.
The party's gains in both chambers of Congress strengthened its ability to oppose legislative measures supporting further U.S. military action in the Middle East.

U.S. President Donald Trump also told CNN that future attacks on Iran were "unlikely" if negotiations progressed over Tehran's nuclear program and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, a major route for global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments.
The peso, meanwhile, remained near the P63-to-$1 level, opening at P63.06 against the dollar Monday.
Because petroleum products are traded in dollars, a stronger peso lowers the local-currency cost of imported fuel, while a weaker peso makes those purchases more expensive.

articles.title: 19-year-old golfer becomes youngest PGA Tour winner in 95 years
articles.summary: Blades Brown became the youngest PGA Tour winner in 95 years Sunday when the 19-year-old rallied from a seven-shot deficit with a 9-under 63 and beat Ben James with a birdie on the second playoff…

image.caption: Blades Brown of the United States poses with the trophy after winning the World Wide Technology Championship on Sunday in Los Cabos, Mexico. (Getty Images)

blocks.text: Golf·Recap

Blades Brown became the youngest PGA Tour winner in 95 years Sunday when the 19-year-old rallied from a seven-shot deficit with a 9-under 63 and beat Ben James with a birdie on the second playoff hole in the World Wide Technology Championship in Los Cabos, Mexico.
Birdies 2nd playoff hole to win World Wide Technology Championship in Mexico
Brown became the youngest winner since Charles Kocsis won the Michigan Open in 1931 when he was 18, a tournament that was considered a regional event in the early years of the PGA.

James lost a four-shot lead going into the final round at El Cardonal at Diamante and then showed his moxie by smoking a 285-yard shot into 20 feet on the par-5 18th and making eagle to salvage a 70 and force the playoff.
But he missed an 8-foot putt on the second playoff hole, and Brown made his 3-footer.
"I'm so obsessed with this game. It tests you in so many ways," said Brown, who graduated high school in January. "I love golf, all the stuff that goes into it and I can't wait for what's next."

For a sleepy FedEx Cup Fall event on the southern tip of Baja California, this was pure theater between two players from the next generation. James was the No. 1 player in the PGA Tour University ranking last season. Brown make a surprising choice to turn pro two years ago while a junior in high school.
Brown was tested even more by going through two bags of golf balls on the range waiting to see if the two-shot lead he had over James would hold, and then going back out to the 18th to decide it.

On the first extra hole, their approach shots were side-by-side, separated by about 3 feet, and both narrowly missed eagle chances. They returned to the 18th tee and their drives were next to each other. Both came up just short of the green.

James nearly holed his pitch and saw it run out 8 feet. Brown, who had a similar pitch in regulation that he hit to 6 feet for a closing birdie, this time came up 3 feet short. James' birdie putt grazed the right edge, and Brown poured in the winner.
They have known each since their junior days and Brown figures this is the start.
"I got him this time, but I'm sure we'll be battling it out for years to come," he said.

With eight players separated by two shots on the back nine, Brown ran off three straight birdies to share the lead and then left the mistakes to everyone else. He hit a superb pitch for birdie on the final hole to post at 23-under 265.
That put him one shot ahead of Michael Kim, who played with the Tennessee teen and made birdie from 12 feet for 64 right before Brown made his putt.

Brown earned his PGA Tour card for 2027 by finishing among the top 20 on the Korn Ferry Tour points list. Now he has a two-year exemption, which puts him in the elite Championship Series when the PGA Tour's new model begins in 2028.
The victory also assures Brown of his first major next year at the PGA Championship.
It was another setback for James, who in 13 starts since turning pro has five finishes in the top five, and two runner-up finishes.

Denny McCarthy, winless in nine years in 240 starts on the PGA Tour, made a 30-foot birdie putt on the 13th hole to take the lead. But he hit a pedestrian pitch to the par-5 14th and had to settle for par. With a wedge in hand from the 15th fairway, he came up some 40 feet short and three-putted for a bogey.
McCarthy's tee shot on the 17th was right of the 18th tee box, he put his next shot off a dirt path into a hazard and made double bogey. He shot 69.
Sudarshan Yellamaraju was the top Canadian, finishing tied for 12th at 17 under.
With files from CBC Sports

articles.title: Pope Leo urges Argentina's Milei to put people before the economy
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV has urged Argentina to protect democracy and ensure economic growth benefits the poor, delivering a message to President Javier Milei over austerity, social welfare and political…

image.caption: Despite a rocky relationship with the Vatican, Milei was all smiles on SundayImage: Tiziana Fabi/AFP/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Pope Leo XIV arrived in Argentina on Sunday, urging to protect democracy and ensure economic growth benefits the poor.
The pope's remarks were widely watched for criticism of President Javier Milei's harsh austerity programs and cuts affecting social services.
While Leo did not address the government's policies directly, he said "the economy must be at the service of the people, rather than people being at the service of the economy."
Talking to Milei and other government officials, he pointed to the plight of those who, "despite hard work, nonetheless struggle to meet their household's needs."
With regards to democracy, he said it was "part of Argentina's heritage that needs to be safeguarded."
The visit to Buenos Aires marks the second leg of the pope's South America tour and is the first papal visit to Argentina in nearly 40 years.

The 71-year old pontiff, who underwent surgery for lung cancer less than a month ago, arrived from Uruguay and is scheduled to visit several cities in the Catholic-majority country before continuing to Peru on Wednesday.

blocks.caption: People were excited about the first papal visit in almost 40 yearsImage: Tomas Cuesta/AFP

blocks.text: Milei's rocky relationship with the Catholic Church
Milei's policies have in the past drawn strong criticism from Argentina's Catholic Church, particularly cuts affecting social services, pensions, disability assistance and public universities.
The Argentine leader, a close ally of US President Donald Trump, has defended his aggressive spending cuts as necessary to stabilize the country's ailing economy and curb inflation.

Annual inflation has fallen from more than 200% to approximately 33% under his administration, but households continue to face financial pressure, and there's been anger over public-sector layoffs and business closures.

In the past, he agressively dismissed criticsm from the Catholic Church, going as far as calling Leo's predecessor, Pope Francis, an "imbecile." He had later though softened his tone and met with Francis in Rome.
On Sunday, Milei struck a significantly more conciliatory note, praising Francis as an "exceptional figure" and the "most important Argentine in history."
Safeguarding democracy
Pope Leo also stressed the need to safeguard democracy in the country.
"Those who exercise authority have a duty to act with prudence, to acknowledge the limits of the power entrusted to them, and to direct their decisions toward the good of the entire community."
The Pope's words carry particular significance ahead of Argentina's presidential election in 2027, in which Milei has said he will seek another term.
The president's aggressive rhetoric and frequent attacks on journalists and political opponents are widely seen as part of an increasing political polarization in the country.
Leo told Milei that strengthening democracy required a "willingness to listen" and the "careful use of words."

His visit marks the first time a pope has traveled to Argentina since John Paul II's trip in 1987. It also brings renewed attention to the legacy of Francis, the country's first pope, who died in April 2025 without returning to his homeland during his 12-year papacy.
Pope Leo starts jam-packed South America tour just weeks after surgery

articles.title: Trump says he was ‘only kidding’ about making UFC’s Dana White next press secretary
articles.summary:
President says it was ‘just a little fun’ to picture White, UFC boss and Trump’s friend, in briefing room with fighters

Donald…

blocks.text: Donald Trump said on Sunday that he “was only kidding” when he announced a day earlier that he had offered the job of White House press secretary to Dana White, the chief executive of the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC).

Speaking to reporters on his way back the White House from his beach club in Florida, Trump explained the premise of his joke, that if the UFC boss, who is a devoted fan of the president, took over the briefing room, flanked by six fighters, reporters “wouldn’t mess around with him so much”.

“So I was kidding, but I think Dana likes the idea, and he is a very capable guy,” Trump added. “Of course, I was kidding. And you could see that because I put all of the great fighters as his assistants, that they’re all going to come with him … It was just a little fun.”

Earlier on Sunday, the president shared an animated AI cartoon made by one of his supporters on social media, which showed UFC fighters beating up journalists and one, Josh Hokit, repeating the racist remark about Michelle Obama he made during the UFC event at the White House on Trump’s birthday in June.

The president said that his mock announcement that White would become his spokesperson, in a social media post on Saturday, “was an example of something where I was kidding, and then people said, ‘You know, that’s actually a pretty good idea’”.
He did not say who, exactly, supported the idea.

The first in a series of taxpayer-funded pro-Trump ads broadcast by the White House in the run-up to the recent midterms closed with images of the UFC fight on Trump’s birthday and remarks about him from White, who could be heard saying: “He is the toughest, most resilient human being I have ever met in my life.” White used that formulation to describe Trump multiple times during the 2024 presidential election campaign, most notably to sing Trump’s praises at the Republican national convention.

The role of White House press secretary has been vacant for three weeks, since Trump’s previous pick, the far-right commentator Katie Zacharia, was forced to resign after trying, and failing, to dodge questions about why she described herself as an attorney despite having failed the bar exam.

articles.title: Nvidia CEO Huang admits affair amid rumors of China spy ties
articles.summary: Following reports of Nvidia's chief Jensen Huang becoming involved with a Chinese spy, Huang offered an apology for cheating on his wife. Meanwhile, the US tech company pledged to investigate the…

image.caption: Jensen insisted he was committed to 'supporting America's national security'Image: Lisi Niesner/REUTERS

blocks.text: US tech giant Nvidia said on Sunday it would investigate claims that its CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by "foreign intelligence efforts."

Multiple media outlets, including The Financial Times, recently reported on American intelligence sharing information on Huang's extramarital affair with a Chinese woman. The woman, according to US intelligence sources, had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security.
Chipmaker NVIDIA profits up, despite trade war challenges

The reports identified her as Alice Huang, an executive for Singapore-based company Megaspeed. The US is investigating the company over suspicions that it was helping Beijing bypass export restrictions and obtain cutting-edge AI chips. According to The New York Times, the company has bought Nvidia chips worth billions of dollars in the last two years.
US lawmakers have invited the Nvidia chief to brief them on the reports.
Nvidia's Huang as rich as Warren Buffet
On Sunday, Nvidia's top executive admitted to being "unfaithful" to his wife of 40 years.
"My actions hurt her and our children," Jensen Huang wrote in an email sent to Nvidia staff. "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."
Nvidia's AI PC explained: AI agents, speed and data privacy
He also said he was he committed to protecting the company and "supporting America's national security."

Huang was born in Taipei and spent part of his childhood in Taiwan before moving to the US. In 1993, he and two other people launched Nvidia, a company that grew to become a leading manufacturer of computer graphic cards and then an essential supplier of computer chips in the AI boom.
Nvidia’s Cage for AI: can it prevent disaster?

The 63-year-old Nvidia CEO is one of the richest people in the world, according to the Forbes magazine, with his $162.2 billion (€145.5 billion) net worth as of Sunday putting him roughly on par with globally renowned investor Warren Buffet.
Huang stays on as Nvidia CEO
In their statement, Nvidia's board of directors said Huang will remain the head of the US-based company while the probe is taking place.
Huang "fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it," according to their statement.
The board said a group of "independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation."
At the same time, the heads of the $4.5 trillion company said they had "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised."

articles.title: North Vancouver soldier who died in Wainwright fire remembered as fearless at funeral
articles.summary: A 23-year-old soldier from North Vancouver was remembered Sunday as a globe-trotting, sporty and car-loving man with an infectious sense of humour and a fearless love for life. A photo of Pte. Aidan…

image.caption: Sonia Monk, Pte. Aidan Goulding's mother, says one of the hardest parts of losing someone so young is losing the opportunity to build on her relationship with him. (CBC)

blocks.text: A 23-year-old Canadian soldier was remembered Sunday as a globe-trotting, sporty and car-loving man with an infectious sense of humour and a fearless love for life.

Hundreds of military personnel, family and friends gathered at an armoury on a stormy day in Vancouver to remember Pte. Aidan Goulding, one of four soldiers killed last month after a grass fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta overtook troops during a training exercise.
His mother, Sonia Monk, described her son as someone with a great sense of humour, always open to a good laugh.
"Whenever I was disciplining him, he would start to laugh or he would try to say something. I could never properly discipline him," she said.
"That's something that our family is going to miss. Nothing is going replace that."
Sonia Monk says Goulding and his fellow soldiers who died in the CFB Wainwright fire "will not be forgotten." (CBC)
Monk said she was proud of her patriotic son who joined the army from a high-paying job.
"When he finally told me, he said, 'I have one life to live, I want to do something important, and so I'm joining the army.' I think that's so unselfish of him," she said.
After he joined the Canadian Armed Forces, Goulding felt like he found a place where he belonged, Monk said.
"It gave him a sense of purpose, a family and a place he truly felt at home."
Goulding's funeral started with soldiers carrying his flag-draped casket into the armoury, with the sounds of a bagpipe cascading, and some words from a rabbi.
Monk described his upbringing in North Vancouver with his brother, Wylder, who was also his best friend.
"They had each other's backs," she said. "Their relationship touched my heart deeply, and I was content in knowing that they would always be close."

items: Funeral mourners recall friendship, dedication of sergeant killed in CFB Wainwright incident
Mother of soldier killed at CFB Wainwright says he wanted to protect Canada

blocks.text: Growing up, he showed his competitive and curious side.
His family said in a statement he played many sports, including soccer and rugby, and developed a love for cars at a young age.
He spent many hours buying used cars, fixing them late into the night under the glow of a lamp on his family's driveway and then reselling them.
The first car he fine-tuned was a used Chrysler 300C.
The modification: make it louder.
"He loved understanding how things worked and took great pride in making them his own," his family said.
He was also stylish.
Monk said her son asked to wear a white suit on his first day of Grade 4. When he turned 21, he asked for a gold suit.
"He was unapologetically himself, and I admired that," she said,
The family has also described Goulding as a globe-trotter.
Sonia Monk, Pte. Aidan Goulding's mother, says joining the Canadian Armed Forces gave Goulding "a sense of purpose." (CBC)
In his short life, he explored many parts of the world, including Mexico, Germany, Austria, Italy, Croatia, Malta, the Netherlands, England and Spain.
Reagan Goulding, his aunt, said during the funeral that he often made those around him laugh.
She said it's been hard knowing that he died at a young age.
"This is perhaps one of the hardest parts of losing someone so young," she said. "It's not just the memories we have lost, but the opportunity to make a relationship we still had time to build."
Reagan Goulding said she could see her nephew, who she described as being "smart, ambitious, determined, and resourceful," perhaps becoming a police officer or joining CSIS.
"I truly believe great things were in his future. We wanted him to know that we all saw this in him, that we believed in him and became a proud follower of him," she said.
She said her last message to Goulding was sent on the day of the tragedy, a text message that said, "Aidan, you better be OK."
She never received a reply.
Who are the 4 service members killed at CFB Wainwright?
Reagan Goulding said if she knew this was her last message she would have said more, including telling him one more time how proud she was.
She also remembered the other soldiers killed in the fire.
They were: Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, B.C.; Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton; and Pte. Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Sask.

"They were young men who matched their calling, who stood beside one another, and who were parts of the family themselves. Their loss is felt by their families, their friends, soldiers, and everyone who has been touched by this tragedy," she said.
"Aidan and his fellow soldiers will not be forgotten," she added.
As the soldiers carried the casket out of the armoury and reloaded it into a hearse to head to the cemetery, the sun broke through the clouds, casting its light over rainy Vancouver.
Monk, who spoke to media after the funeral, said she felt it was a sign from Goulding, encouraging her to move forward with life.

"Because I think through tragedy or hardship, he would always say things like that, 'We'll move forward.' So, I think that's what he was sort of saying to me today, actually, with the sun shining bright in my eyes."
Monk said she felt "supported and lifted" after hearing stories from Goulding's "brothers and sisters" in the army.

"I'm quite tired, I haven't eaten a lot, I haven't slept a lot. But all the support and seeing everybody here today, it's remarkable. I can't find a word other than remarkable," said Monk, adding that "There's lots of love in Canada."

articles.title: Doctor who treated victims of Krakow shooting speaks to the BBC

"We rushed into the area and started our rescue" before the emergency services arrived, Pędziwiatr said.

articles.title: Man charged with murder over fatal stabbing of HungryPanda delivery rider in Melbourne
articles.summary:
Footscray man charged over death of 47-year-old Feng Jianming in the CBD on Friday night

  • Get our breaking news…

blocks.text: A man has been charged with murder after a delivery rider was stabbed to death while working, leaving his family bereft and a city in mourning.
On Friday night, HungryPanda delivery rider Feng Jianming, 47, and another rider confronted a man allegedly tampering with their bikes in Melbourne’s city centre.
An altercation ensued and the man, a 51-year-old, is alleged to have stabbed both riders.
Emergency services rushed to the scene on Frederick Way, but Feng could not be saved.
The second rider, 34, was taken to hospital with serious injuries, where he remained on Monday.
The 51-year-old was arrested by police on Saturday and on Monday morning was charged with one count of murder and intentionally causing serious injury.
Feng, originally from China’s Shaanxi Province, had been in Australia for about nine years.
His wife, Xu, their four parents and two children all relied on his hard work to get by at home.
The news of Feng’s death reverberated through Melbourne and gig worker communities in Australia and abroad.
Mourners left floral tributes and notes near the state library over the weekend in his memory.
Some cards expressed sympathy for his family, while others vented grave frustrations with messages such as “city of criminal” and “Asian lives matter”.
A GoFundMe fundraiser set up by the Melbourne Chinatown Business Association had raised almost $390,000 by Monday morning to help Feng’s family with emergency travel and funeral expenses.
Food delivery company HungryPanda said it was assisting the family with visa arrangements, funeral expenses, financial support and insurance.
The 51-year-old man was remanded in custody to appear before Melbourne magistrates court on Monday.

articles.title: Aramco Tower hit in heart of Saudi capital as Houthis launch fresh strikes
articles.summary: Footage authenticated by BBC Verify shows damage to the building in the capital's central financial district.

blocks.text: The Aramco Tower, a skyscraper in the Saudi Arabian capital's central financial district, had been hit by an air attack.
A statement issued via the Houthi-controlled Saba news agency confirmed the group had targeted Riyadh's business zone on Saturday, without mentioning the Aramco Tower by name.
The Saudi energy ministry said the tower had suffered only "minor damage" and no one had been killed or injured.
Footage authenticated by BBC Verify shows more extensive damage to the building, with at least one floor appearing to have been badly hit by a missile or drone strike.
Windows on more than one level appear to have been shattered by the strike.
The Houthis also said Riyadh's airport and Aramco oil storage facilities were targeted in separate strikes. Saudi Arabia said its air defences had intercepted and destroyed several missiles.
The strikes were the latest claimed by the Yemen-based armed group against targets deep inside Saudi Arabia, which the Gulf power has struggled to contain in recent months.
It came a day after the Houthis accused a Saudi-led coalition of killing at least 33 people, including women and children, in an air strike on Yemen.
Footage broadcast by Houthi-run television channel Al Masirah showed rescuers pulling bodies from the rubble of several buildings in al-Shariyah, a town to the east of the capital, Sanaa.
Saba said 39 people had been injured in the strike. Saudi Arabia has not commented.

A Saudi-led coalition has been fighting the Houthis for more than a decade in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government, which has lost control of a large swathe of the country to the rebel group.
Although the conflict had largely been dormant in recent years, fighting has intensified following the outbreak of the Iran war.

An informal ceasefire unravelled in July after the Tehran-backed Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they have called a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport Saudi Arabia said had been to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing there.
Major fighting has since resumed between Houthi forces and troops aligned with Yemen's Saudi-backed government.
The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed.
